title: Morris Ramen to close this month
text: Subscribe Today! Archive Newsletters Francesca Hong of Morris Ramen Over seven years, one State Assembly campaign and countless bowls of ramen, this King Street institution served the community more than just noodles.  Contributing Writer Francesca Hong of Morris Ramen It’s easy to miss Morris Ramen at 106 King St. Compared to some of its flashier neighbors in the happening food-and-drink corridor of King St. — Lucille, Plain Spoke Cocktail Co. and more — its curb appeal is far lower key. The interior is cozy — a bar and banquette comprise all the seating. The lights are low. Light wood accents, plenty of plant life and a black-and-white tile backsplash behind the bar combine to create a comfortable, friendly atmosphere. Since it opened in late 2016, the restaurant has been a go-to for fans of the traditional Japanese noodle soup. Its come-as-you-are familiarity is part of what's kept locals and visitors coming back for years. Step inside, and you feel like you've been there before — like you're part of the community. You can taste the love in the food. That’s because opening the restaurant was a dream of its owners, State Rep. Francesca Hong and Matt Morris. But, “to be real,” Hong and Morris said in a post on Morris Ramen’s social media pages Tuesday morning, “dreams die.” In the post, titled “A farewell letter from Morris Ramen,” the co-owners announced that the restaurant would be closing for good. Their last service will be Saturday, Feb. 24. The restaurant has withstood some of the most significant moments and struggles in the lives of its owners and the restaurant industry in recent years. Around the time Morris Ramen opened, Hong and Morris welcomed a son, George, who the couple watched “grow up running up and down the bar of the shop then stop in at a neighboring business to say hello” they said in Tuesday morning’s post. In March 2020, Hong and Morris closed the restaurant temporarily due to COVID. Faced with what she saw as “a failure of leadership that trickled down,” per a 2021 Madison Magazine interview , Hong became a spokesperson for the Wisconsin restaurant industry, authoring a statement to Gov. Tony Evers demanding emergency unemployment benefits and tax breaks to buoy struggling businesses and employees. It was this failure of leadership to look out for local businesses which led her to run for a seat in Wisconsin’s State Assembly. Since 2020, Hong has represented Wisconsin’s 76 th District. Hong was named Madison Magazine’s Chef of the Year in early 2021. Later that year, Bon Appetit magazine included her on a list of “Heads of the Table,” a group of trailblazing leaders in the American restaurant industry. “There were no economic safety nets to catch us when our doors closed,” said Hong in an interview with Bon Appetit of her disappointment in the government’s COVID response. “I knew that something had to change." Despite the challenges of the pandemic, community support for the restaurant has seemed relatively constant. In 2022, the “Ramen Rescue” GoFundMe campaign raised over $50,000 largely to cover debts incurred during the pandemic. Nicole Schmies, Matt Morris’s sister, organized the campaign on behalf of her brother. Though Tuesday’s post didn't offer a specific reason for why the restaurant was closing now, Morris and Hong emphasized “it has been an extraordinarily taxing couple of years. I think we are broken in ways we can’t really comprehend yet.” In the post, the owners thanked “all our staff, past and present, for being the heartbeat of our restaurant,” along with their customers. “The reason we are loved in this community is because of your support, your cards, your kind words on socials and your trust” the post read. Throughout its existence, Morris Ramen served the community more than just noodles. During COVID, the restaurant participated in the Cook It Forward program, or CIF, through which struggling restaurants were paid $10 per meal; the meals were then donated for free to those in need. With Hong’s help, CIF raised over $100,000 in donations in around six months. Morris and Hong ended their message Tuesday with a call to continue that community service. “Our wish is that we as a community remain hopeful and safe. That we continue to keep our hearts open and take care of one another.” Jess Miller is an editorial intern for Madison Magazine. ​COPYRIGHT 2024 BY MADISON MAGAZINE. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. title: New noodle shop gives us a reason to slurp
text: Subscribe Today! Archive Newsletters New noodle shop gives us a reason to slurp New noodle shop gives us a reason to slurp Morris Ramen brings delicious noodles to King Street.  Former Editor in Chief New noodle shop gives us a reason to slurp The Backstory : Shinji Muramoto found two people as passionate about ramen as he is in former Restaurant Muramoto chefs and spouses Matt Morris and Francesca Hong, whom he then helped to open Morris Ramen on King Street. The small downtown noodle shop has been a hot spot for signature ramen bowls. The Vibe : Located in the former home of the original Restaurant Muramoto, Kushi Bar Muramoto, The Haze and then Red Sushi, Morris Ramen was redesigned mostly by Morris and his father Bob Morris with the help of Carlson Construction. Jacob Morrison is the architect who designed the space. The smell of ramen fills the air as you walk into the small space and take a seat on a wooden block chair. “We wanted people to come in how ever they were and feel comfortable and happy and cozy,” says Hong. New noodle shop gives us a reason to slurp The Menu : The small menu offers four bowls, including two misos, a spicy chicken bowl and the signature Morris bowl with chashu pork belly. Non-ramen offerings, like the chicken wings and an ice cream sandwich, are simple and well executed. The Must-Try : The miso bowl is Morris’s favorite, and there’s a story behind it. Two years ago, Muramoto sent Morris to Obihiro, Japan–Madison’s sister city. There, Morris worked for three months in a small restaurant and really got into miso ramen. Morris set out to create a miso bowl that would impress Muramoto, who was born in Sapporo, Japan, known for its miso. The challenge resulted in two versions on the menu–one with ground pork, corn and moyashi, and a veggie version with seasonal items, aburaage and nori. The Bottom Line : A lot goes into making ramen, and they do it justice. “To serve something so humble and so filling as ramen … it’s so fulfilling to see people come through the doors and walk out happy,” says Hong. 106 King St., 416-5547 Andrea Behling is managing editor of Madison Magazine. title: Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series
text: Subscribe Today! Archive Newsletters Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series Late-night collabs bring new items to the menu  Contributing Writer     Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Photo by Erica Krug Francesca Hong, chef and co-owner of Morris Ramen , had so much fun making ramen with guest chef Maggie Roovers of Forequarter during Madison Area Chef Network’s Chef Week in March, that she decided to do it again. And again. And again. Announcing Morris Ramen’s “Guest Chef Late Night Ramen Series,” Hong invites different chefs to join her in the kitchen once a month on Thursday nights from 9 p.m. to midnight to cook up steamy bowls of ramen never seen before on the Morris menu. “I wanted to feature different cooks around town who also want a creative outlet,” Hong says. “A lot of us make the same things every day, so it’s fun to make something different and work with different people. I think this idea of collaboration will be really good for our community and I wanted to run with it.”   Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series Morris Ramen officially kicked off the series on Thursday, April 26, when Hong invited Megan Travers and Michael Signorelli of Each Other to join her in creating a $25 prix fixe menu for guests including two bowls of ramen– one created by Hong and one by Signorelli — and a dessert from Travers. Travers, former head baker and pastry chef for Underground Food Collective, recently started working for El Grito Taqueria and new venture Mijo Frozen Treats. Signorelli has a background in whole animal butchery and is also a cook at Casetta Kitchen and Counter. Each Other is Travers and Signorelli’s side project with Jacob Wolf and Tim Smith; the foursome prepares food for pop-ups and special events like last summer’s Makeshift Festival at Olbrich Park. Travers says she and Signorelli got to know Hong from eating at Morris and from Hong eating at Casetta Kitchen. “We’re big fans of Morris,” Travers says, “and it’s always a good time collaborating with friends from other restaurants and different backgrounds.”   Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series For April’s late-night ramen feast, Hong prepared a shio (salt-based broth) ramen with chicken, mustard greens and purple daikon. (A vegetarian version of Hong’s ramen was available — calling ahead to make this request is helpful.) Signorelli created a cumin lamb ramen with lamb meatballs, scallions and chili oil. Travers says the guest ramen dish was inspired by their love of Szechuan food, calling the broth “a bit of a barnyard brawl made from lamb neck, chicken feet and pork neck bones.” For dessert, Travers served a toasted coconut fudge bar with a kinako (roasted soy bean flour) shortbread crust and sorghum vinegar caramel. “Sorghum vinegar has become a kind of staple around our house,” Travers says. “We usually cook steak with it or use it in a braise, but its fruity, almost chocolatey acidity goes well with sweets too.” Expect a $25 set menu each month with two bowls of ramen and an additional item like a side of pickles, dessert or a beverage depending on who’s in the kitchen. Grab a seat at the bar facing the open kitchen and listen in as each chef takes a turn explaining their dishes to restaurant staff right before 9 p.m. “I don’t know anything about ramen,” Signorelli jokes as he explains his entree. “I eat it here and that’s it.” As customers start rolling in, Hong and Signorelli take turns scooping broth and plating garnishes. Although it’s a little hectic, the vibe of guest chef night is playful. Ten minutes into service, Hong suddenly shouts out “How could I forget?” Those within earshot look concerned until she points her phone at the overhead lights which start flashing different colors. “Rainbow lights!” Hong says.   Morris Ramen kicks off guest chef series Look for the next guest chef night on May 24 featuring Molly Maciejewski, executive chef of Madison Sourdough. Dan Jacobs and Kristen Schwab of Milwaukee’s DanDan , an American-Chinese restaurant in the Third Ward, will join the Morris Ramen crew on June 24 and Matt Schieble of Mint Mark will spin off-theme a little and make pho, a Vietnamese soup, on July 12. “We look forward to working with people who are as passionate and excited about ramen as we are and are looking to collaborate,” Hong says. title: Madison360: Mayor Dave ponders response to attacks on Madison
text: "The War at Home," an Oscar-nominated documentary about Madison during the Vietnam War, was released in 1979. The film depicted violent protests and a famous and fatal campus bombing. Today, the title feels relevant again, as the Republicans who are poised to run state government seem to despise Madison — and all it represents — in ways that border on the pathological. Granted, picking on Madison has long been fashionable, most famously by Lee Dreyfus, the Republican governor who joked that the city is a certain number of square miles "surrounded by reality." Madison's Spencer Black, a Democratic representative retiring after 26 years in the Legislature, says he knew floor debates were going his way when foes started trashing his town. "Whenever I had someone beat, their only counter argument was that, ‘Oh, that's what they think in Madison.' I knew I had the debate won," he muses. "It was sort of the last refuge for scoundrels to link an idea to Madison." And it may have felt playful last winter when Sen. Glenn Grothman, a West Bend Republican, suggested that the state take over snow removal in Madison to force us to use more salt, or last summer, when Rep. Steve Nass, a town of LaGrange Republican, threatened legislation to ban the European-style pavement markers for bicycles the city had installed. Play time, my friends, is over. "People have been running against Madison forever, but they haven't been doing it with the same vehemence and the same edge" as now, observes Mayor Dave Cieslewicz. Incoming Gov. Scott Walker and majority Republicans have rejected $810 million in federal money for high-speed rail linking Madison and Milwaukee, opposed efforts to convert the Charter Street heating plant on the University of Wisconsin-Madison campus to burn biofuels, threatened the future of embryonic stem-cell research at the university, and signaled opposition to domestic partner benefits. And then there's their declaration of war not only on public employee unions, but on all public employees. In a truly cringe-worthy anecdote, a headline on Monday's Wall Street Journal editorial page heralds a " Badger Rebellion ," lavishing praise on Walker for courageous "reforms" aimed at ending public employee collective bargaining rights. In case you haven't noticed, the Journal under Rupert Murdoch has become an ever-more vitriolic enemy of ordinary Americans and an even-more ardent and unapologetic advocate for billionaires. Black, who has long represented many UW and other state employees and championed environmental causes, says: "I am still on the job and still get constituents' calls, and boy, am I hearing from constituents. They are concerned about what will happen to their retirement benefits and are thinking of leaving much sooner than they otherwise would." Beyond benefits, he says "many are not very optimistic about what kind of policies they will be asked to carry out." He adds: "Most public employees, despite the Republican rhetoric, are motivated by public spiritedness." The number of employees requesting pre-retirement meetings increased to 1,539 in November compared to 1,254 from the same month a year earlier, says Matt Stohr of the Department of Employee Trust Funds, which administers the state's retirement program. He estimates there are 90,000 to 95,000 active workers in the public retirement system in and around Madison. Black and Cieslewicz agree that the central theme for them is not liberal versus conservative, but new economy versus old economy. "Some of it is almost a fear of the future," Black says. "It is reactionary in the truest sense of the word. When Scott Walker can say that losing $810 million is a victory, I hate to see what a defeat would look like." Cieslewicz, who was uncharacteristically emotional in public remarks last week about the loss of train money, concurs. "Well, Madison is much more connected (economically) to the real world than folks like (Walker and others) seem to understand," he says. "We are hitched to the world economy. So much of the rest of the state is falling behind that. I don't want to be condescending to the rest of the state. It is just reality that the new economy is based on ideas." The mayor adds that "the guys who will be running the state may say they believe in free markets, but apparently do not believe in the free market of ideas. They are pursuing policies that are shouting to the world, ‘Please stop, don't progress. We really like 1950.'" Cieslewicz has a point. When listening to the preferred GOP future, it reminds me of "Happy Days," the sit-com set in 1950s Milwaukee that offered an idealized vision of a long-ago time. Cieslewicz says he understands some level of animosity toward Madison, "but the answer isn't to make Madison more like the rest of the state, but to make the rest of the state more like Madison. And I don't say that because I am the mayor, but because we represent the new economy." He complains that Republicans are driving a "deeper and deeper wedge" and while he sees how that helped them politically, the election is over. He also says he understands some resentment of public workers, whose "fundamental deal" is to forego benefits from economic upswings for safety on the downside. "It is all about stability," he says, accusing Walker of using state and UW workers as scapegoats. That said, he advises public employee unions to be less inclined to react bombastically. Still, after failing to get Walker to even discuss the train decision, Cieslewicz is thinking about adopting a more adversarial style himself. "I am actually in the process of figuring out where I want to be on that continuum," he says. "My feeling out of the box was I wanted to reach out to Walker. But I am re-evaluating. Does the city and state need a voice who is full-throated in opposition to these horrible, regressive policies? Is that being responsible to my job? Am I going to reap more pain for Madison if I do that?" Yet, he asks rhetorically, "What is the point of pulling my punches? This is not just a political game. They are pursuing policies that are so repugnant and so ignorant that it is hard to get your head around it." Happy days, indeed. Become a Cap Times member today and enjoy great benefits. title: Mayor Paul Soglin wins eighth term as Madison mayor
text: Madison mayor Paul Soglin speaks at an election night party at The Brink Lounge on East Washington Avenue on Tuesday. The numbers were not close . Soglin received about 72 percent of the vote while challenger Scott Resnick only managed 27 percent. Madison's 'mayor for life' defeated opponent Scott Resnick 72 percent to 27 percent.  Madison mayor Paul Soglin speaks at an election night party at The Brink Lounge on East Washington Avenue on Tuesday. The numbers were not close . Soglin received about 72 percent of the vote while challenger Scott Resnick only managed 27 percent. Paul Soglin won re-election as Madison mayor Tuesday with an overwhelming percentage of the votes, beating opponent Scott Resnick and stepping into his eighth term. “I really believe in Madison and that we can be the best city in the world,” Soglin said, “that we can be the place to solve all of these problems and earn that number one ranking in every single category, for every single resident.” Resnick said it was a tough evening, but that there are not many 28-year-olds who get the opportunity to run against such a long-time mayor. “To be in this position at this age is phenomenal,” Resnick said, “even though tonight is a tough one.” The numbers were not close. Soglin received about 72 percent of the vote while Resnick only managed 27 percent. “That’s a rousing endorsement of Paul’s tenure to date and the promise of the future,” said Stu Levitan, a longtime political activist and Soglin supporter. Resnick called Soglin early in the night to concede with about half the results in. Soglin took to the microphone shortly after for a rather subdued victory announcement. “We’re doing this a little early and the reason is I want to get to bed because I’ve got to get up tomorrow morning and work on committee appointments for the next two years,” Soglin said as he opened his speech. Although Resnick largely kept on pace with Soglin for fundraising, including adding $50,000 to his own campaign, Resnick said his campaign faced an “uphill battle” coming out of the primary. The race also drew little public interest and was overshadowed by other major events, include state politics. For the near future, Resnick said he’s not thinking about politics, though he is still involved in a number of civic projects. “I truly enjoyed every moment serving the public, (it’s) something I am going to miss,” Resnick said. Moving forward, Soglin said his number one priority is to take the various programs already underway and make sure that they follow through and meet those commitments. “I think he’s got some things that he wants to finish and he will finish and that are good for the city,” said District 2 Ald. Ledell Zellers. Soglin said he plans to drop unemployment, for all populations, down to what’s considered statistically complete employment, around 2 percent. He also wants to see the 1,000 affordable housing units completed, the end of veteran homelessness and cooperation with the school district leading to academic success in every school in the city. “The city of Madison is going through a journey,” Soglin said. Looking from 2019 back to 2011, he said, residents are going to witness significant transformations demonstrating that the city addressed the challenges of poverty and disparity, creating opportunities for success for everyone. Part of that issue will be tackling racial disparities, particularly in light of the death of Tony Robinson, a 19-year-old black male who was shot and killed by a police officer in March. “The tragedy of Tony Robinson’s death has galvanized the city of Madison to address many of these issues,” Soglin said. “It’s unfortunate that it takes that kind of tragedy to get us aligned, to get us moving in the right direction.” Long-time Soglin supporter Brenda Brown said her number one focus now is for Madison to address its racial issues and become a role model for the country. “I know that we have what it takes here in the city of Madison to make it happen,” Brown said. And as for whether Soglin will be able to, she said: “I don’t know anybody who could do it better.” One frequent critique of Soglin during the campaign, however, was his failure to work with City Council and Dane County leadership. Asked whether he would change that moving forward, he said that analysis was wrong. “That’s Scott’s perspective,” Soglin said, citing his commitments to voters as reasons for some of the disagreements, particularly around the budget. And as for why he has continued to run for the job, Soglin said it’s largely to make Madison better. “The feeling of satisfaction when something goes right, when you see the differences, you see the change, when you see the performance at school improve, when you see the new housing and what it means to change a neighborhood, the feeling of success in those instances is immensely gratifying,” Soglin said.  Bryna Godar joined The Capital Times in 2014, where she primarily covers city and county government. She previously worked for the Rochester (Minn.) Post-Bulletin and the Minnesota Daily. title: Opinion | Former mayor quietly working on Madison preservation
text: Mary Ellyn and Joe Sensenbrenner Dave Zweifel: Joe Sensenbrenner and his wife, Mary Ellyn, continue to improve the city with efforts to preserve places like Troy Farm and Gardens and McPike Park.  Editor emeritus Editor emeritus Mary Ellyn and Joe Sensenbrenner Joe Sensenbrenner, Madison's mayor from 1983 to 1989, hasn't been on the front pages in recent years, but both he and his wife Mary Ellyn have been as active as ever helping make Madison a better place. That's why I was glad to see Community Shares of Wisconsin honoring this outstanding Madison couple last week with their annual Liesl Blockstein Community Leadership Award. For decades, the couple have been active, often with their own resources, in preserving open spaces for public use. The Sensenbrenners have worked through the organization now known as Rooted to preserve places like Troy Farm and Gardens, McPike Park in central Madison and several properties in Milwaukee. They have long been a guiding force behind the unique middle and elementary charter school and neighborhood center on the South Side known as the Badger Rock Center. Through Rooted, Mary Ellyn and Joe continue to connect the community through food, land and learning, the Community Shares citation noted. Incidentally, Mary Ellyn served several terms on the board of directors of the Cap Times Kids Fund, determining where grants would be distributed to deserving nonprofits that work on the problems and challenges of young people in our community. Community Shares, the umbrella organization that raises funds for dozens of nonprofits that promote social and economic justice, also honored Joyce Hall, the program coordinator for Freedom Inc., with its Sally Sunde Family Advocate Award, and Ximena Linares-Rodriguez of the Tenant Resource Center with the Linda Sundberg Civil Rights Defender Award. She has been instrumental in assisting Spanish-speaking tenants navigate the rental market. Denise Matyka, who for 40 years has been active in everything from Community Shares to the National Organization of Women and was a national organizer for the Equal Rights Amendment, received CSW's lifetime achievement honor. title: Wisconsin Police Shoot, Kill Man Who Allegedly Pulled Knife on Them: Video - AOL.com
text: 0 Mud Lord via Storyful Police officers in Madison, Wisconsin, sparked controversy Wednesday ... after they shot and killed a man who was being detained in the middle of the street, and the moment was captured by a bystander on video. The shocking clip shows four officers wrestling with a man in the street, attempting to pin his arm back and subdue him. In an attempt to subdue the man, it appears one officer pulled out a taser ... informing her fellow officers by yelling out "Taser! Taser! Taser!" so as not to hit her comrades with an electric shock. Seconds after the man was being tased, several gunshots are then heard, and the man's body goes limp. This individual has not been identified by authorities yet, but has been described as a male in his early 30s. Advertisement Madison Police Chief John Patterson says officers shot and killed the man after he pulled out a fixed blade and injured an officer. The state's Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing the shooting. Patterson also warned citizens not to judge this shooting based on only one video angle, asking them to reserve judgment until authorities come to a full determination of what happened. Here is a different angle of the shooting obtained by WISN News . None of the officers were wearing body cameras during the incident ... which will certainly add to the growing controversy around the shooting.

title: Wisconsin protesters demand justice for man shot dead by police - AOL.com
text: 2 By Daniel Trotta July 23 (Reuters) - Hundreds of protesters gathered for a vigil in Madison, Wisconsin, on Thursday, demanding police be held responsible one day after an officer shot dead a man in an incident that bystanders captured on video. The shooting death of Corey Ruiz, whom local community advocates and Wisconsin media outlets identified as Black, went viral on social media, reigniting some of the outrage that surfaced after the 2020 police killing of George Floyd in Minnesota and other killings that have raised questions of racism in police use of force in the United States. Police said Ruiz was armed with a knife that injured at least one of the four officers who wrestled Ruiz to the ground. During the struggle, an officer drew his handgun and fired what sounded like three shots at close range, according to the video. Late on Wednesday demonstrators gathered at the scene and at the Capitol, where an outdoor concert was canceled because of the protests. Demonstrators returned to the scene on Thursday, placing flowers in the street. Organizers introduced relatives of Ruiz, including a daughter, to the crowd. Advertisement Earlier Thursday, several protesters interrupted a press conference by Madison Police Chief John Patterson, demanding that the officers be jailed. The protesters held signs such as "Corrupt cops deserve to die, too!!!" Video from Wednesday shows four uniformed officers grappling with the man amid shouts of "Let go" and "He's got a knife." At some point an officer used a Taser to try to subdue the man, but for unknown reasons it was unsuccessful, Patterson said. Police had stopped Ruiz in connection with reports of a person looking into parked cars. Another call at the same time about an unlawful entry into a home may have increased the police presence, Patterson said. The Wisconsin Department of Justice's Division of Criminal Investigation is conducting an independent homicide investigation, Patterson said. (Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Vista, California; Editing by Donna Bryson and Christopher Cushing)

title: Wisconsin Police Shoot, Kill Man Who Allegedly Pulled Knife on Them: Video - AOL.com
text: 0 Mud Lord via Storyful Police officers in Madison, Wisconsin, sparked controversy Wednesday ... after they shot and killed a man who was being detained in the middle of the street, and the moment was captured by a bystander on video. The shocking clip shows four officers wrestling with a man in the street, attempting to pin his arm back and subdue him. In an attempt to subdue the man, it appears one officer pulled out a taser ... informing her fellow officers by yelling out "Taser! Taser! Taser!" so as not to hit her comrades with an electric shock. Seconds after the man was being tased, several gunshots are then heard, and the man's body goes limp. This individual has not been identified by authorities yet, but has been described as a male in his early 30s. Advertisement Madison Police Chief John Patterson says officers shot and killed the man after he pulled out a fixed blade and injured an officer. The state's Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing the shooting. Patterson also warned citizens not to judge this shooting based on only one video angle, asking them to reserve judgment until authorities come to a full determination of what happened. Here is a different angle of the shooting obtained by WISN News . None of the officers were wearing body cameras during the incident ... which will certainly add to the growing controversy around the shooting.

title: Second Harvest sends near 52,000 meals to Fox Valley tornado victims - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Second Harvest Food Bank of Southern Wisconsin is sending two semi trucks filled with food to its Feeding America partner in eastern Wisconsin. The two trucks are carrying 63,000 pounds of food, the equivalent of approximately 52,000 meals, to communities in northeast Wisconsin. Among the 25 volunteers who helped load the trucks is John Kuech, who lived in the Fox Valley area for nearly three decades. “Well, I can get emotional about it. I, you know, we lived there for 28 years. Our kids grew up there,” Kuech said, “so It was pretty devastating to see that.” Kuech and his wife have volunteered with Second Harvest for more than three years. When they learned food was being sent to the area they once called home, they signed up to help. “But we heard they were going to be doing this for the Fox Valley. And we thought we should come back and help.” Kuech said, “Because of our contacts there.” President and Executive Director of Second Harvest, Michelle Orge, said hunger can increase the challenges families face in the aftermath of disaster. “Hunger makes everything harder and when anybody is affected by a disaster, they still need to eat,” Orge said, “What this means to them is one less thing to think about at a time when so many other things are already happening.” Second Harvest said when one food bank is impacted by a disaster, others across the Feeding America network step in to ensure families have access to food, regardless of distance. Local businesses in the Fox Valley have also been working to feed families impacted by the tornado.
